items.title: Singapore defends status as a ‘trusted business hub’ after the U.S. proposes extending AI chip controls to Southeast Asia
items.summary:
The U.S. proposed tighter export controls on AI hardware on Monday (Nov. 16), mandating licenses for firms looking to ship advanced chips to four Southeast Asian nations: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

The rule change comes days after reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, a cloud computing firm which allegedly funneled over $7.5 billion of Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms via its regional subsidiaries. (Megaspeed says it is cooperating with U.S. inspections and denies wrongdoing)

The new rule also requires large data centers anywhere in the world to get a license if it wants to offer computing power to companies based in China.

Singapore, where Megaspeed is headquartered, is now trying to defend its reputation.

“Singapore is a trusted international business hub, underpinned by a strong rule of law,” a government spokesperson wrote in a press statement dated Nov. 16 . “We take our international reputation seriously and do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries.”

The country added that it is engaging U.S. authorities to review details of the new measure, while working with affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses. 

Thailand Vice Minister for Commerce, Kirida Bhaopichitr, told CNBC that they were ‘prepared’ for the new rule. “We don’t want to be a hub for transshipment of these goods from the U.S. to China, so we’ll more closely scrutinize these companies, especially data centers.”

Indonesia, too, said it was reviewing the…
items.t: Singapore defends status as a ‘trusted business hub’ after the U.S. proposes extending AI chip controls to Southeast Asia

items.title: U.S. labor force may come to resemble China’s army of one-man companies due to AI, says Bill Gross—leveling wealth inequality and national debt
items.summary:
Though more than six in 10 Americans want to run their own companies, many just don’t know where to start. Serial entrepreneur Bill Gross has got more than a million business concepts ready to launch, and he’s sharing them for free.

Gross is the founder of Idealab, one of the longest-running tech incubators, launched in 1996, with 45 IPOs and acquisitions to its credit. Gross, who made his fortune building software, has since launched Idealab Studio—an AI-powered platform providing startup ideas, support, and investment.

The founder of education software provider Knowledge Adventure has set some tough targets for success: He wants to create 100 million jobs, countering the expected wave of AI job losses using the very technology that displaced workers. Gross believes a boom in American entrepreneurship could help offset wealth inequality and macroeconomic headwinds, such as the growing national debt.

“I had this dream of making a million companies,” Gross tells Fortune on the sidelines of the Web Summit conference in Lisbon. “I was pitching this to a group of investors, and they told me that China has 30 million one-person companies. 

“I think we could have 30 million one-person companies in the United States, and if you had 30 million one-person companies, that would really do a lot for taxation. That would do a lot for income equality, and that would do a lot for not having people near the bottom worried about where they stand relative to the people at the top.” 

AI can be used as a “leveling tool,” Gross adds: “I hope there could be 30 million companies that are…
items.t: U.S. labor force may come to resemble China’s army of one-man companies due to AI, says Bill Gross—leveling wealth inequality and national debt

Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

items.title: Voters want relief from rising power bills. Democrats must find a way to deliver without stalling the AI investment helping drive the economy
items.summary:
When Democrats won both houses of Congress in the blue wave of November’s midterm elections, some of them did so partly on the strength of campaigns featuring sharp criticism of the AI boom , and particularly the proliferation of gigantic data centers across the nation.

Sherrod Brown won back his Senate seat after calling his Ohio opponent “the face of data centers.” As Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s next senator, put it: “People really effing hate data centers.” Indeed, of 41 local data center measures on midterm ballots in 10 states, voters sided against the industry in 40. And in a March Gallup poll, 71% of Americans opposed a data center in their area, well above the 53% who opposed a nuclear plant.

Some Republicans—likely hearing the same opposition from their constituents—have distanced themselves from the president’s pro-AI rhetoric. In fact, opposition to runaway data center development may be a rare bipartisan stance .

It’s a classic “pocketbook issue”: Wholesale electricity prices near some data centers have risen as much as 267% in five years, according to a Bloomberg analysis, and data center operators are paying for only about 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth , according to Cornell researchers. Meanwhile, the steady drumbeat of dire predictions about how AI will put us all out of work—if it doesn’t decide to kill us—haven’t helped the hyperscalers’ reputation.

Fear and fury over AI may have helped hand Democrats wins, but it also created a conundrum for them and their colleagues across the aisle: What will they—what can they—do about it?…
items.t: Voters want relief from rising power bills. Democrats must find a way to deliver without stalling the AI investment helping drive the economy

items.title: Honeywell CEO says AI isn’t about replacing workers as C.H. Robinson touts 60% productivity gains: ‘We all have to reskill ourselves’
items.summary:
Honeywell Technologies CEO Vimal Kapur says AI isn’t about replacing industrial workers. What it will do, though, is force them to quickly adapt as the technology transforms how companies operate.

“It’s about making humans more productive,” Kapur said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Sharing the stage with Kapur was C.H. Robinson CEO Dave Bozeman, whose 120-year-old logistics company has already seen productivity gains of more than 60% since the end of 2022 as it uses AI and other technologies to automate repetitive tasks.

The two CEOs spoke about how AI is transforming some of America’s largest industrial companies, even as the technology fuels anxiety among employees worried their jobs could eventually disappear. 

Both CEOs told Fortune ’s Andrew Nusca that AI has the potential to make workers more productive, but that it will also require them to learn new skills and rethink how they’ve traditionally done their jobs.

Changing jobs 

Honeywell is no stranger to change. The industrial giant has operated across a wide range of industries during its 140-year history. In the past two years alone, it has spun off both its advanced materials business and aerospace division to focus on industrial automation. Now, Kapur is using AI to transform its business once again.

While much of the attention around industrial automation has focused on AI-powered humanoid robots, such as Tesla’s Optimus, and its potential to replace factory workers , Kapur sees a broader opportunity to help employees do their jobs more effectively.

He argued AI could be…
items.t: Honeywell CEO says AI isn’t about replacing workers as C.H. Robinson touts 60% productivity gains: ‘We all have to reskill ourselves’

items.title: How Airbnb cofounder and US Design Chief Joe Gebbia fixed a $100 million government problem for $1.5 million
items.summary:
For two decades, Washington tried to drag its federal retirement process out of the paper age. Contractors poured millions into the effort, but the system stayed bogged down in paperwork. Then Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia showed up with a handful of engineers and, by his account, did in six months what the government had struggled to do for 20 years.

Gebbia, now the country’s first chief design officer, said the effort dates back to 2002, when federal records were digitized under President George W. Bush. The government had tried and failed for two decades to move retirement online, he said.

“There’s about $100 million spent on contractors that produce nothing,” Gebbia told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell on Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit . His team, he said, brought the retirement application process online for roughly $1.5 million.

The overhaul was an early win for Gebbia, who arrived in Washington in 2025 knowing little about federal retirement. The system ran on paper, with personnel files kept in a limestone mine in western Pennsylvania , and some retirees waited months for their full pension benefits. It also became his proof of concept for a much bigger job: fixing how Americans deal with their government online.

Bringing Airbnb’s playbook to Washington 

Gebbia never expected to work in government. He was serving on Tesla’s board and running Samara, his prefab backyard-home startup , when a text from Elon Musk in January 2025 invited him to hear about the problems federal agencies were struggling to solve. One issue in particular…
items.t: How Airbnb cofounder and US Design Chief Joe Gebbia fixed a $100 million government problem for $1.5 million

items.title: ‘A complete evaporation of confidence’–6 critical things Nvidia, and interim CEO Colette Kress, need to nail on the first Jensen-free earnings call
items.summary:
Nobody—not even Nvidia’s board—knows who will lead the new regime at Nvidia now that Jensen Huang is gone . For now, longtime CFO Colette Kress is in the driver’s seat as interim chief, and she’s been handed Atlas’s job of holding up the sky during Nvidia’s fiscal 2027 third quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. 

Kress has to be the “voice of stability” while she also attempts to get the investment community reoriented to the fundamental issues at Nvidia that impact the business and valuation of the stock, said Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global.

First and foremost, analysts are still expecting a typically gargantuan quarter, with $109.3 billion in revenue, according to S&P’s Visible Alpha consensus—which is routine for Nvidia and will be mission critical for Kress. The quarterly figure is up about 92% from $57 billion last year, but the number has to be delivered in the right way. Nvidia’s gotten the world used to over performance and now the company needs to sizzle with confidence at one of the most vulnerable moments in its history.

“There’s a complete evaporation of confidence at the moment, and there’s so much uncertainty around a lot of qualitative issues,” said Otto. “The narrative needs to come back to fundamentals. How is the business doing? Is it achieving what it said it’s going to achieve?”

Nvidia’s stock is down 20% since the company’s last quarterly earnings on August 26, losing roughly half a trillion dollars in market cap, amid a broader selloff in AI and related tech stocks that have since rallied. Tuesday could be a…
items.t: ‘A complete evaporation of confidence’–6 critical things Nvidia, and new CEO Colette Kress, need to nail on the first Jensen-free earnings call

items.title: Newly reelected Sen. John Hickenlooper sketches Democrats’ AI line: race China, but regulate frontier models like nuclear weapons and airplanes
items.summary:
Sen. John Hickenlooper wants American AI to win in the international AI arms race. He just isn’t sure it needs to be able to rebuild itself without limits.

“Maybe we don’t need recursive learning, unlimited,” the Colorado Democrat told Fortune’s Diane Brady on Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, where he teleconferenced in. He described machines “reinventing themselves sometimes outside the fence line of their domain that they’re supposed to stay in.”

“That should cause real concern,” Hickenlooper said.

Hickenlooper, a member of the Senate Commerce Committee, won his second and last term two weeks ago, leading Republican state Sen. Mark Baisley 61% to 35% on election night. While his seat was expected to go his way, eight seats won Democrats control of the Senate in last Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which data centers and the AI buildout was one of the most referenced issues that influenced voters’ decisions. 

His comments come as the buildout continues and as AI companies use their models to speed up their research. In September, more than 20 researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, published a paper warning that automating AI research could set off an “intelligence explosion.” Alan Chan, one of its lead coauthors, said that valid safety mechanisms aren’t in place.

Hickenlooper said he isn’t against the labs moving fast. “They are pushing as fast as they can. I understand that, and that’s good,” he said, referencing the international rivalry. “We want to make sure that our frontier AI is the best in the world because it has the…
items.t: Newly reelected Sen. John Hickenlooper sketches Democrats’ AI line: race China, but regulate frontier models like nuclear weapons and airplanes

items.title: Michigan’s next governor hasn’t talked to Trump yet—but wants to work with him on a 50% auto tariff set for her first day
items.summary:
Michigan Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson hasn’t spoken to President Donald Trump since winning the state’s governor’s race as part of the blue tsunami that swept across the nation earlier this month.

“Not yet, but I intend to,” Benson said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit in an interview with Fortune editorial director Kristin Stoller. “We’ve all got to work together to better our economy, to better Michigan.” 

Top of mind, though, is a tariff that could land on her first day in office. After negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down in August, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian-made cars, trucks, and parts to 50% beginning Jan. 1, 2027. That’s the same day Benson takes over from term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. 

Benson said she hopes for opportunities to collaborate, “first and foremost, in reducing the impact of these tariffs.” She recalled touring auto parts distributor Detroit Axle in October, where she said the owner told her: “I’m sending millions of dollars into paying these tariffs, and it’s money that I had saved to expand my business, to create more jobs.” 

Last year, Detroit Axle said it might have to shut down a warehouse and lay off more than 100 workers, although it later backtracked. But owner Mike Musheinesh told the Associated Press, “It’s a market of who is able to survive; it’s not a matter of who can thrive.”

Benson said a governor can uniquely go to Canada and broker a Michigan-specific agreement to protect jobs and lower costs, something she promised to pursue on the campaign trail. She also said she…

items.title: ‘We’re having to overcome brand America’: Kraft Heinz CEO says made-in-U.S.A. designation is more ‘complicated’ in appealing to Canadian customers
items.summary:
As U.S.-Canadian relations go frosty, one American food brand is having to be more intentional about appealing to its northern neighbors.

Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane said the made-in-the-U.S.A. moniker doesn’t carry the same positive connotation as it did in decades past. As a result, he said, the Chicago- and Pittsburgh-based food giant—behind Jell-O, Lunchables, and Heinz ketchup—is having to tweak its messaging.

“Brand America is not as strong as it once was, and that’s been the case for some time,” Cahillane told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “We’re having to overcome brand America. Whereas, in the ‘50s, ‘60s, ‘70s, into the ‘80s, brand America was a badge of honor, it’s a little bit more complicated today.” 

Ongoing trade tensions, including a 50% tariff on $20 billion of Canadian goods , have chilled Canadian attitudes towards American productions, as have repeated threats from U.S. President Donald Trump about making Canada the “ 51st state ,” claiming it relies too heavily on the U.S. economically. While Canadians have continued to pour money into U.S. investments , many have also made a concerted effort to boycott American goods in favor of Canadian counterparts. 

In some areas, these boycotts are taking a toll on the U.S. economy. A report from the Canadian government published last month found that despite Canadian visitations to the U.S. beginning to increase, visitations from Canadians are 29% lower as of September 2026 than they were two years ago. According to the…

items.title: Days after Microsoft and the FAA went dark, Chase and Wells Fargo customers can’t get to their money
items.summary:
If you had trouble logging into your bank’s website on Monday, you’re not alone. JPMorgan Chase customers spent much of the day unable to log in or move money, with the bank saying the outage spread from it’s website and app to some branches and to outside apps that connect to Chase accounts. Wells Fargo , Capital One, and Zelle also had problems with their online banking platforms as customers reported trouble.

Reports started Monday morning and climbed quickly. Downdetector logged nearly 4,500 Chase reports shortly after 1:30 p.m., most of them about website logins. By 2:22 p.m., the count had passed 20,000.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson told Fortune . “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

Customers described a wider disruption than that statement suggests. Comments on Downdetector mentioned problems with ATMs and in-person systems as well as online banking and Zelle. Some customers opening the Chase app got a message reading , “Some services aren’t available.”

Ashley Lutz 

The problems also reached apps outside the bank. Plaid, which links bank accounts to payment, investing and budgeting apps, said its own network was working normally but that it was seeing connection problems with Chase accounts. Customers trying to link or refresh a Chase account through another app may have gotten errors as a result.

Downdetector listed Chase, Wells Fargo, Capital One and Bank of America among the banks with spikes in…

items.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration

Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes.

This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words.

items.title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year
items.summary:

Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.

The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.

Boots is to start prescribing medical cannabis, it has announced, in a first for a UK high street pharmacy.

The online service is being offered to patients in the UK aged 25 and older who have an eligible condition such as chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia.

items.title: ‘Strangers gave me £2,409’: the online community helping people in debt
items.summary:
People come together online to support one another with small voluntary donations to ease financial worries

For some time people struggling with debt have used social media to document what they owe, swap advice and hold themselves accountable as they try to pay it off. Some have built large audiences around their repayment journeys, using views and engagement to generate income through creator payment schemes, livestream gifts and donations from followers towards their debts.

Now the idea is being taken a step further: rather than one person building an audience to help clear their own debt, strangers are creating communities to help pay off one another’s.

items.t: ‘Strangers gave me £2,409’: the online community helping people in debt

items.title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
items.summary:
PM to meet European leaders at summit this week aiming to secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’

Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.

It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.

Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.

It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

items.t: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU

items.title: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham
items.summary:
Alan Milburn’s review will mark a watershed moment for our approach to welfare and childhood. This is how I’m determined to create change

  • Report: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis

A generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians.

We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too.

Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

items.t: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham

items.title: When the boss has an affair, the whole family business can pay the price

Fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair is the latest reminder of the shared toll paid when patriarchs cheat

From Profumo to Petraeus to Gary Hart, Bill Gates and Bill Clinton, history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. Now we have the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang.

These men – smart, respected, powerful – make decisions that simply baffle the rest of us. If they’re so intelligent, how could they not see how things were going to end up? The answer is they’re men. And when there’s a younger woman who shows interest, well …

items.title: Bad jobs or benefits? Milburn should force employers to help the young | Richard Partington
items.summary:
Long-awaited final report will call for benefit cuts but lack of entry-level jobs is also driving the crisis

  • ‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking

A generation is being sold short. Almost a million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Austerity and the Covid pandemic cast a lengthy shadow, AI is upending the jobs market, and the cost of living is soaring – all under the microscope of the social media age.

On Tuesday, Alan Milburn’s final report on young people and work will bring Britain to a fork in the road: either continue on this path of state and market failure or sharply change direction.
